Pregnancy

Swollen hands in pregnancy: comfort measures and warning signs

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Rings feeling tighter can be an early clue that your fingers are swelling. Pregnancy changes fluid balance, and mild puffiness can become more noticeable later in the day. The important distinction is between a gradual familiar pattern and a sudden change or symptoms affecting how your hands work.

Call promptly for a sudden change

Contact your maternity team immediately if swelling suddenly increases, particularly in your face or hands. Do not wait to see whether a home remedy brings it down.

A severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting or feeling very unwell adds to the concern for preeclampsia. You do not need to confirm high blood pressure yourself before calling.

Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or a seizure. A suddenly painful, hot or markedly one-sided swollen limb also needs urgent assessment.

Make room for swelling before jewellery becomes tight

Remove rings while they still slide off easily, and loosen watches or tight cuffs. Swelling can increase over the day even if something fitted comfortably in the morning.

If a ring becomes stuck and the finger is painful, numb, pale or blue, get urgent help to remove it. Do not keep pulling against an increasingly swollen joint.

Resting your forearms on a pillow and gently opening and closing your hands may feel more comfortable. Avoid forceful massage or tightly wrapping a swollen hand.

Tingling may mean pressure on a nerve

Pregnancy-related fluid retention can compress the median nerve where it passes through the wrist. Carpal tunnel symptoms include tingling, numbness, pain or a weaker grip, often worse overnight. The thumb, index and middle fingers are commonly affected.

Tell your clinician if you are dropping objects, losing strength or have persistent numbness. These symptoms deserve more than reassurance that swelling is normal.

A properly fitted splint that keeps the wrist neutral at night may help. Adjust repetitive tasks and take breaks from prolonged wrist bending. A physiotherapist can advise on suitable movement and positioning.

Support comfort without trying to flush fluid away

Pregnancy increases circulating fluid and changes how fluid returns from tissues to the circulation. Pressure from the growing uterus and gravity can make swelling worse later in the day. This does not mean all swelling is beneficial or that swelling is what opens the pelvic joints for birth.

Drink regularly and follow any fluid advice given for your own medical circumstances. Forcing large quantities of water is not a proven treatment for swollen fingers.

Eat a varied diet. Swelling by itself does not diagnose potassium deficiency, and adding supplements or large amounts of one food is not an appropriate correction without assessment.

Severe salt restriction is not recommended solely to prevent pregnancy-related hypertension or preeclampsia. Ordinary healthy eating advice and a specific treatment plan should not be confused.

Celery, cabbage, herbal teas, oils and products sold as natural diuretics are not established treatments for pregnancy hand swelling. Concentrated herbal products can have uncertain safety; check them before use.

Bananas, vegetables, fruit and lean protein can form part of a balanced diet; choose less heavily processed food when practical. Artichoke or ginger is not a prescribed diuretic, and dandelion, coriander or fennel teas and mustard or flaxseed oil massage have not been established as treatments for this problem. A food being familiar does not establish the safety of a concentrated herbal preparation.

Follow pregnancy caffeine guidance for its pregnancy-related effects, rather than treating caffeine avoidance as a proven cure for swelling. Do not start water tablets, potassium supplements or concentrated herbal products without a clinician’s advice.

Choose comfortable rest and movement

Gentle regular activity may be helpful if your pregnancy team has not advised a restriction. Swimming can be enjoyable for some people, but it should not be presented as a guaranteed hand-swelling treatment.

From 28 weeks, settle to sleep on your side. Either the left or right side is acceptable; you do not have to maintain the left side all night. If you wake on your back, simply turn to your side.

Compression stockings may be considered for leg symptoms in appropriate circumstances, but they do not treat swollen hands. Ask about the problem you actually have rather than borrowing an unrelated remedy.

Comfortable shoes and cuffs that do not leave deep pressure marks may help when your feet are also swollen. If leg compression is prescribed, ask about correct sizing and when to put it on, often before swelling builds during the day.

Keep watch after birth

Swelling and carpal tunnel symptoms often improve as the body adjusts after pregnancy, but there is no promise that everything disappears within a few days.

Preeclampsia can first occur after delivery, including in someone whose pregnancy blood pressure was normal. New severe headache, visual symptoms, sudden hand or face swelling or breathing problems still needs urgent attention.

Arrange follow-up for persistent numbness, weakness or swelling. Using pillows and adjusting feeding or baby-care positions may reduce strain while your hands recover.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS advises immediate maternity contact for sudden swelling, especially with headache, visual changes, upper abdominal pain or illness, because pre-eclampsia can be present.

NICE advises against salt restriction solely to prevent hypertensive disorders. NHS sleep guidance accepts either side from 28 weeks, and hand symptoms may need carpal-tunnel care.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record the timing of swelling and any hand numbness or weakness. Your maternity team can assess the cause and tailor comfort measures.

When to seek help

Sudden face or hand swelling needs prompt maternity advice. Severe headache, visual change, severe upper abdominal pain, breathing difficulty, chest pain or collapse requires urgent or emergency care, including after birth.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sudden hand or face swelling needs prompt maternity advice.
  • Tingling and weak grip may indicate carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Avoid self-prescribed diuretics and unrealistic fluid-flushing remedies.

Frequently asked questions

Must I sleep only on my left side?

No. After 28 weeks, go to sleep on either side; turn back onto your side if you wake on your back.

Will the swelling definitely disappear within days of birth?

No. Recovery varies, and new or worsening postpartum symptoms still need assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
